summary: A self-deploying, radiation-shielded inflatable habitat and four-point thermal gradient power recovery system for continuous Lunar and Martian surface operations
details:
What It Does & How It Works:
This Phase I conceptual engineering architecture introduces an autonomous, deployable surface enclosure for the Moon and Mars. It resolves three critical exploration bottlenecks: solar power deprivation during Lunar nights and Martian dust storms, cosmic radiation hazards (SPE/GCR), and abrasive electrostatic regolith dust.

  • Phase I (Pressure-Differential Self-Deployment): Pre-packed at Earth atmospheric pressure inside a sealed canister, the flexible elastomer-metallic radiation canopy deploys automatically upon exposure to the near-vacuum of the Moon or low-pressure Martian atmosphere without heavy cranes, anchoring via passive electrostatic adhesion.
  • Phase II (Four-Point Thermal Gradient Energy Recovery): Exploits extreme temperature differentials across four thermal nodes (Outer Exposed Skin, Inner Shadow Enclosure, Internal Ground Regolith, and Subsurface Core at 30–40 cm depth) to drive a closed-loop Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) or Solid-State Thermoelectric Generator (Seebeck Effect) for uninterrupted day-and-night power.
  • Phase III (Dual-Chamber & Electrodynamic Dust Shielding): Pairs a transparent solar chamber protected by active traveling-wave EDS dust repulsion with a hardened, radiation-shielded operations chamber.

Benefits, Impact & Creativity:
Unlike rigid habitats or purely solar-dependent bases, this mass-efficient architecture guarantees continuous operational survivability for both human crews and autonomous assets (such as NASA’s RASSOR excavators) independent of solar visibility.

Tools & Methodology:
Developed using thermodynamic cycle modeling, space radiation attenuation principles, and NASA open planetary environmental datasets. Permanently archived on Zenodo (DOI: doi.org) under CC-BY-4.0.
